title: Automatic thought journal
description: This article explores the practice of keeping an automatic thought journal, one of the key tools in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). We’ll explain how to correctly record and analyze automatic thoughts to reduce emotional discomfort and prepare the ground for working through core beliefs.

texts: One of the key goals of CBT is working with your thoughts.
Automatic thoughts are like “compact” versions of your beliefs; they reflect the deeper layers of your thinking.
Before you can work with a thought, it’s important to notice and record it.
In this chapter, you’ll be introduced to a powerful tool for self-discovery — the automatic thought journal (also known as an ABC journal).
<important>This isn’t just a notebook for sad entries; it’s your personal “detective” that helps you understand the reasons behind your mood and teaches you how to manage it.</important>
The journal shows the connection between what happens (the situation), what we think (thoughts), and how we respond (emotions, sensations, and behavior).
Because of this, it consists of several key sections:
• Event: a brief description of what triggered your emotional reaction.
• Thought: the automatic thought that arose in response to the situation.
• Emotions: the feelings you experienced at that moment.
• Reaction: your behavior or actions in response to those emotions.
• Adaptive response: a more helpful thought or perspective on the situation that helps change your emotional reaction.
Let’s break down each section.
Event
Here, we briefly describe exactly what triggered the unpleasant emotions.
It’s important not only to outline the situation but also to be as specific as possible.
For example, a phrase like “my mom hurt my feelings” is too general — it’s better to specify exactly what she said or did.
And instead of saying “I did a bad job,” it’s better to be specific: “I made a mistake in the report.”
A trigger can be an external event or internal sensations, thoughts, or memories — the main thing is to keep your descriptions clear.
Automatic thought
This section is about how you interpret a situation.
To notice your thoughts, ask yourself: “What am I thinking right now?”
Identify the most significant and emotionally charged thought.
If the wording is too general, refine it to be more specific.
Rate how much you believe this thought on a scale from 0 to 10.
For example, if the “Event” section says “I made a mistake in the report,” your thoughts might be: “I’ll never do anything right,” “I’m a failure,” or “Making mistakes is stupid.”
Choose the thought that resonates most strongly, write it down, and rate your belief.
Emotions
Before this section, ask yourself two questions:
• What emotions was I feeling? (sadness, anger, anxiety, guilt, fear, shame, etc.)
• How intense were these emotions? (0–10)
For example: sadness — 9, despair — 7, low mood — 5.
Physical sensations
Here, you record physical reactions during intense emotions — how your body responded to what you were feeling.
Be specific: it could be a lump in your throat, a cold sweat, a heavy feeling in your stomach, etc.
Behavior
Describe what you did after the thoughts and emotions appeared.
What actions followed?
Behavior might include things like crying or snapping at colleagues.
Adaptive response
In this column, analyze the original thought and formulate a more adaptive, supportive response.
These questions can help:
• How realistic is this thought?
• What facts support it, and what facts contradict it?
• What are the worst, best, and most likely outcomes?
• What happens if I keep believing this thought? And what would change if I reconsidered it?
For example, instead of “I’ll never be able to do anything right,” you could say: “I’ll fix the mistake and learn from it. After all, everyone makes mistakes.”
Your journal also helps you track cognitive distortions.
Let’s take a quick look at what they are.

<important>Cognition refers to the processes of perception and thinking (thoughts, images, ideas) that occur in our minds. Cognitive distortions are errors in how the brain processes information.</important>
They prevent us from thinking logically and rationally, causing us to perceive reality in a distorted way.
If you notice a cognitive distortion in your thoughts, label it.
If not, don’t worry — just skip this section for now.

texts: Why keep an automatic thought journal?
Journaling is key to deep self-awareness: it helps you better understand your emotions, thoughts, and behavior.
Regular entries allow you to see recurring patterns that influence your mood and actions.
The act of writing helps develop mindfulness.
You’ll start to notice which thoughts arise in different situations, making it easier to manage your reactions.
Support for therapy (and beyond): your entries are valuable material for self-reflection.
They are useful both when working with a psychologist and for independent practice.
Why is it important to keep entries?
What isn’t written down is easily lost in the depths of memory.
We often think we can keep everything in our heads — but we’re usually wrong.
<important>Reflection — the ability to analyze your experiences — develops when we formulate our thoughts and put them into words.</important>
This way, we don’t just preserve important ideas, we also gain a deeper understanding of ourselves.
Secrets to effective journaling:
• Consistency is key: a journal isn’t a magic wand; it requires practice. Log your entries regularly to see results.
• Catch the moment: write down your thoughts and emotions as soon as they arise. This makes it easier to “catch” automatic thoughts before they slip away.
• Progress, not perfection: don’t chase an ideal. Every small win is a step forward.
Journaling is a skill that takes time to master.
Be patient with yourself and give it time to become a habit.
